beyond-your-beat-1f8b184ee4.headline: 'Operation Economic Outcast': US sanctions two Mumbai firms, five Indians over alleged Iran oil trade
beyond-your-beat-1f8b184ee4.fulltext:
The United States on Thursday imposed sanctions on two Mumbai-based companies and five Indian nationals over their alleged involvement in the trade of petroleum products from Iran, as Washington stepped up its economic pressure on Tehran.
The US department of state targeted SSPL Solutions Private Limited and Samudra Marine Services Private Limited for allegedly facilitating the import of petroleum products from Iran.
The action also blocked five individuals associated with the two firms from carrying out transactions related to their respective companies, according to news agency PTI.
Two people linked to SSPL Solutions, Dhwani Vora and Nisarg Vora, were sanctioned, while Ketan Kochikar, Bhupendrasingh Sahu and Harishyam Hariharan Chundakattil, associated with Samudra Marine Services, were also targeted.
US expands sanctions over Iranian petroleum trade
The sanctions against the Indian entities and individuals are part of the US crackdown on Iran under “Operation Economic Outcast”.
“The department of state is sanctioning ten entities, six individuals, and five vessels in connection with trade in Iranian-origin petroleum, petroleum products, and petrochemical products,” the US state department said in an official statement.
The department alleged that the targeted entities channelled millions of dollars to the Iranian regime, strengthening what it described as one of Tehran’s most important revenue streams and enabling its continued illicit conduct.
“The US government is imposing sanctions on both the buyers and sellers driving this trade in Iranian petrochemical products,” the department said.
At the same time, the US authorised wind-down transactions involving Samudra Marine Services until October 23.
A wind-down period allows parties to complete existing transactions and exit operations before sanctions or liquidation measures fully take effect.
Treasury targets 17 entities and shadow fleet vessels
Separately, the US treasury department sanctioned 17 entities and their associated shadow fleet vessels as part of the same effort to restrict Iranian oil revenues.
“Treasury is starving the tyrannical regime in Tehran of the money it uses to wage war in the region, and we will continue exposing those who enable the regime’s oil sales,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said.
“No enabler of Iranian sanctions evasion is safe from the full force of Treasury's authorities,” he added.
A Treasury official told reporters that the measures represented what the department described as its “most significant blow yet to Iran’s remaining illicit maritime infrastructure”.
“Today's action represents the most significant blow yet to Iran's remaining illicit maritime infrastructure by neutralizing the vast majority of the shadow fleet,” the official said.
According to Reuters, the Treasury official said the operation was aimed at cutting Tehran’s funding for the war, missile construction, cyberattacks and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).
Pressure on Iranian oil exports
The latest sanctions come after the US reimposed its blockade of Iranian ports on July 14 following the breakdown of a memorandum of understanding between Washington and Tehran.
A Treasury official said Iran had about 20 million barrels of crude oil remaining on vessels outside the blockade. The global oil market consumes about 100 million barrels per day.

beyond-your-beat-af8da1d16e.headline: Nobel Prize in Literature goes to Canadian author Anne Carson
beyond-your-beat-af8da1d16e.fulltext:
The 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature is awarded to the Canadian author Anne Carson “for her bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature,” the Swedish Academy, Stockholm, said on Thursday (October 8, 2026).
Anne Carson published a series of notable works in the 1990s. Throughout her entire authorship, Ms. Carson, with a light touch, explores the possibilities of writing, a process by which the literary sketch has become of particular value to her.
‘The Beauty of the Husband: A Fictional Essay in 29 Tangos’, published in 2001, tells of a cutting and sardonic row with a deceitful husband, its 29 episodes each opening with lines of verse by the romantic poet John Keats. Keats’s sublime words about beauty being truth are, in brutal yet playful fashion, juxtaposed with this exhausting relationship drama.
The permanent secretary of the Swedish Academy, Ingrid Carlberg, said she had briefly spoken to Ms. Carson.
“We didn’t have so much time to speak. All she had time to tell me was that she is for the moment in Iceland, where she’s listening to the wind. She was taken by surprise but was very happy. I could hear that in her voice,” said Ms. Carlberg.
Among these is ‘The Glass Essay’ in ‘Glass, Irony, and God’ (1995), which demonstrates the potential of the long poem where genre boundaries are seen to blur.
Almost all her literary production has centred upon the intersection between the philologist’s obsession with words and the poet’s desire for new meaning. She has herself identified the etymology of words as the starting point for all her work.
It singled out her poem “Nox,” printed on one continuous sheet of paper in homage to her dead brother, as “an unforgettable work”.
Ms. Carson has been mentioned as a possible Nobel laureate for years.
Born in 1950 in Toronto, Canada, Ms. Carson published her doctoral thesis in Classics entitled ‘Odi et Amo Ergo Sum’ in 1981 and has, throughout her entire career, combined poetry writing with translation work and teaching at various universities.
Last year, the Nobel Prize in Literature was awarded to Hungarian writer László Krasznahorkai for his works on “apocalyptic terror.”
The announcement of medicine Nobel kicked off the Nobel announcement week. Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann, and Georg Nagel have been awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for discoveries leading to a technique called optogenetics, which allows scientists to control select nerve cells using light.
Belgian-American particle physicist Francis Halzen is the recipient of Physics Nobel for his contributions to IceCube, a neutrino observatory in the South Pole, and for the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin.
The Nobel Prize in Chemistry was given to Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai for untangling mysterious mirror images in molecules, a discovery that has been used to develop countless drugs.
The Nobel Peace Prize will be announced tomorrow (October 9, 2026). The Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences, popularly known as Economics Nobel will be announced on October 12.
The winners will get a cash award of 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.2 million). The award will be presented on December 10, the Nobel Prize day, also the death anniversary of Swedish inventor Alfred Nobel, who in his will dictated that his estate should be used to fund “prizes to those who, during the preceding year, have conferred the greatest benefit to humankind”.
(With AFP inputs)

other-interests-e2bff1ba2b.headline: ‘Delights await!’: Margaret Atwood and other writers on Nobel winner Anne Carson
other-interests-e2bff1ba2b.fulltext:
Margaret Atwood
Anne Carson’s work has long been admired among poets of many countries. For new readers, I would recommend The Beauty of the Husband – direct and visceral, funny and angry and sad – or Men in the Off Hours. Delights await!
Emily Wilson
Many congratulations to Anne Carson for the well-deserved Nobel prize! This is also great news for translation, classics, poetry, the breaking of generic and disciplinary boundaries, and the fact that you don’t have to fit a pre-existing mould to have a brilliant, successful career.
Ocean Vuong
To see the Nobel Committee honour a mind and spirit of such immense capacity and rigour gives me hope for the role of letters in our world at an hour when the vocation’s integrity is more threatened than ever before. For decades, Carson’s unapologetically erudite work has centered strangeness and mystery as methods of human revelation. And its myriad and restless formal enactments have granted endless permissions to multiple generations of writers. Like the best work out there, it fosters others as it forges new ways to be and think for itself. I count myself lucky to write in its wake.
Rebecca Perry
In 2013, I (and pretty much every writer I knew at the time) went to see Anne Carson give the Poetry Society annual lecture. She had us gripped, of course; she was generous, smart, sharp, impeccable in cowboy boots and a suit. Her person demands undivided attention. At the end, in the Q&A, a man asked a long, self-indulgent question to which she simply replied: “No.” The audience waited, briefly, for elaboration. None came.
And there lies the magic of Anne Carson – she is concurrently at play and utterly serious. She never gives many words when one will do.
For most of my writing life she has been the writer I go to for pretty much anything I need. I pick up The Beauty of the Husband and I fall in love with poetry again, I deal out the pamphlets of Float and remember that ambition and weirdness are good, I teach The Glass Essay and it shows up notions of formal boundaries as an absurdity.
She shows us that there is always, that there must be, room for risk and vision, for uncompromising writing. Poets everywhere are rejoicing.

world-b68c227f15.headline: 'Bold and inventive' Canadian poet Anne Carson wins Nobel Literature Prize
world-b68c227f15.fulltext:
'Bold and inventive' Canadian poet Anne Carson wins Nobel Literature Prize
- Published
Canadian poet, essayist and translator Anne Carson has been awarded this year's Nobel Prize in Literature.
Carson, 76, is celebrated for works that often cross the boundaries between poetry, fiction and scholarship.
The Nobel Prize committee said they had selected her "for her bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature".
Carson responded by joking that the judges were "crazy" for honouring her. "I think they're all crazy... Well, you know, it's crazy," she told public broadcaster RUV in Iceland, where she is currently staying.
The Nobel Prize is awarded for a lifetime's body of work and is regarded as the most prestigious award in global literature, with the winner receiving 12 million Swedish kronor (£900,000, $1.2m).
Ingrid Carlberg, permanent secretary of the Swedish Academy, said she had broken the news to Carson on the phone shortly before the public announcement.
"She had time to tell me was that she is, for the moment, in Iceland, where she is listening to the wind," Carlberg, said.
"She was taken by surprise but very happy. I could hear that in her voice."
Born in Toronto in 1950, Carson lives in Michigan and has also held Icelandic citizenship since 2022.
Anders Olsson, chairman of the Swedish Academy's Nobel committee for Literature, praised the way Carson has "broken away from lyrical poetry bound to the narrative self and inspired new forms of contemporary literature".
"This method of writing leads to playful and ironic works that move not only between classical and modern poetry but also between different genres and artforms," he said.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Carson's win was "an extraordinary achievement and a proud moment for Canada".
The writer's works feature "wit, imagination, and a style entirely her own," Carney wrote on social media.
"She has brought ancient stories to new audiences and transformed the way we think about literature."
'Outstanding importance'
Carson's notable works include The Glass Essay, Autobiography of Red: A Novel in Verse, Nox, Float and The Beauty of the Husband: A Fictional Essay in 29 Tangos.
In 2019, her performance piece Norma Jeane Baker of Troy drew a line between famous beauties from different historical periouds - Helen of Troy and Marilyn Monroe.
In 2021, she released The Trojan Women: A Comic, a graphic retelling of Euripides' ancient story; and her translation of Elektra by Sophocles was staged starring Brie Larson in London last year.
She has been a professor of classics for more than 30 years and her writing is often inspired by Greek literature.
Her translations have often given a contemporary twist to ancient works.
"Her collaborations with visual artists and choreographers and with opera and theatre directors demonstrate the freedom with which she relates to literary expectations and rule systems," Olsson said.
"It is this that lies behind the outstanding importance her work since the 1990s has had for the international art and literature scene."

India to Unveil AI Regulation Blueprint Within 30 Days, Minister Says
India is accelerating its push to govern artificial intelligence, with the government set to publish a consultation paper outlining a regulatory framework within the next month. The announcement, made by Union Minister for Electronics and Information Technology Ashwini Vaishnaw on Thursday, marks a concrete step toward formal rules for a technology that is spreading rapidly across the economy and society.
Speaking at an event centered on a World Bank report on AI, Vaishnaw said the paper would serve as the foundation for future legislation, with a heavy emphasis on industry accountability. He directed his department to produce a document focused primarily on the safety implications of AI deployment.
"Secretary Krishnan spoke about AI regulation, yes, time has come. I request the department to come out with a regulation focused consultation paper which focusses on safety, that is the most important point, safety related to AI use," Vaishnaw said.
The minister outlined five broad priorities that will anchor the proposed framework: safety, a human-first approach, skilling, inclusion, and addressing societal harms caused by AI. He set a clear timeline for the release.
"In a month's time we should be able to publish the consultation paper," he said, adding that it would form the basis for subsequent regulation.
Industry to Shoulder the Bulk of Risk Management
Vaishnaw made clear that conventional legislation alone would be insufficient to manage the risks posed by advanced AI systems. He reiterated the government's long-standing position that a "techno-legal" approach is required, blending technological safeguards with legal measures and active participation from the private sector.
"We have always maintained that AI and technologies cannot be regulated just by having a law. We have to bring a techno-legal solution," he said.
The minister signaled that technology companies will be expected to take on considerable responsibility for managing risks associated with their systems. He specifically pointed to cybersecurity, user safety, deepfakes, and psychological harm as areas where the industry would need to lead.
"Bulk of the responsibility will have to be taken by the industry, especially on cyber security, on safety, on user harm, on psychological disorders that might come and on deepfakes," Vaishnaw said.
His remarks place industry accountability at the heart of the government's proposed approach, even as the precise regulatory obligations and enforcement mechanisms remain to be outlined.
Deepfakes and Psychological Risks in Focus
Among the risks highlighted by the minister, deepfakes received particular attention. Vaishnaw warned that increasingly sophisticated AI-generated content could mislead users and create wider societal consequences. He described deepfakes as a form of harmful output that could cause significant problems as their quality and believability continue to improve.
"People believe them and the quality of deepfakes is increasing every day," he said, warning that such content could create misleading narratives and influence people into taking harmful decisions.
Vaishnaw also called for psychological risks associated with AI use to be explicitly addressed in the consultation paper.
"Many of these harms are also related to psychological disorders which come because of the way AI can lure people. So please include that also in your consultation paper," he said.
The proposed framework will also examine how AI adoption can remain inclusive, particularly as the technology creates uneven economic and social benefits. The minister acknowledged that while some sections of society stand to benefit substantially from AI-led productivity and economic gains, others could feel excluded from the transition.
A Long-Building Regulatory Push
The move has been anticipated for months. In July, MeitY Secretary S. Krishnan said the government was considering a separate legal framework for AI and that the time was right to start looking at dedicated legislation. In January, Vaishnaw had already articulated the need for a techno-legal approach to deal with issues such as deepfakes and other risks.
Sudeep Shrivastava, COO of the IndiaAI Mission, has also argued that India should have a say in discussions over AI safety standards. He said those rules should not be shaped only by the US and China, given that they will affect other countries as AI becomes more widely used.
The Indian announcement coincides with a broader global regulatory push. The same day Vaishnaw outlined the Indian plan, privacy officials in the United Kingdom opened an investigation into advanced computer programs and secured safety promises from ten global software builders.
Infrastructure and Talent Development Plans
Alongside the proposed regulatory framework, Vaishnaw outlined the government's plans to strengthen AI infrastructure and public-sector adoption. He said the Centre estimates demand for 10,000 graphics processing units (GPUs), with the first tender covering 5,000 GPUs.
"Our demand estimate is for 10,000 GPUs and the first tender that we are coming out is for 5,000," he said.
The government is also pursuing five-year supply agreements intended to provide companies with greater demand visibility and encourage longer-term investments in AI infrastructure. Vaishnaw said the department had issued a request for empanelment the previous day as part of the procurement initiative.
For AI adoption across government departments, the Centre plans to establish an empanelment mechanism through which eligible AI models, solutions and startups can qualify to participate in departmental tenders.
"It won't be a tender process. It will be an empanelment process," he said, explaining that selected companies would subsequently be able to bid for government projects requiring AI technologies.
On the talent development front, Vaishnaw said the government has worked with industry to prepare an updated curriculum for AI-related education, which has been shared with the Ministry of Education. Joint workshops involving the ministry and industry are expected to help universities and colleges adopt the revised curriculum.
The minister also highlighted examples of AI applications delivering measurable gains in agriculture, healthcare and dairy production. In Baramati, he said, the combination of satellite information, IoT sensors, weather intelligence and farm-level data had helped increase sugarcane yields by 40%, while reducing labour costs by 20-40% and water and fertiliser use by 30%.
Similarly, he said AI-enabled agricultural services in Gujarat were being used by more than five lakh farmers, while an AI application serving the dairy ecosystem was benefiting 26 lakh milk producers and covering three crore cattle.
Domestic GPU Ambitions
Vaishnaw also indicated that India is working towards developing domestic GPU capabilities, particularly for AI inference, over the next three to four years. He said a clearer technological roadmap had recently emerged under the country's semiconductor efforts, making it possible to pursue an Indian alternative for certain AI computing requirements.
According to the minister, the roadmap had not been discussed publicly earlier because the path towards developing such capabilities was not sufficiently clear.
"But now that roadmap is visible and we can say that in three to four years time frame, India, our talent pool which has the capabilities will be able to come up with a solution which can become a good solution for the country and for the global sector," he said.
The minister added that further progress on the initiative would be shared in the coming weeks and months.
India currently relies on foreign computer models because the country lacks the servers and chips needed to build its own powerful software. The push for domestic GPU development is part of a broader effort to reduce that dependence.
Vaishnaw argued that AI's economic value would increasingly come from practical applications that help individuals and smaller businesses access capabilities previously available mainly to larger enterprises. He also pointed to the potential of smaller, fine-tuned open-weight AI models to deliver better results than frontier models on narrowly defined tasks.
While describing India's AI journey as promising, the minister cautioned that scaling the technology would involve social, technical and regulatory challenges. The government's forthcoming consultation paper, he indicated, would seek to balance the benefits of broader AI adoption with safeguards addressing risks to individuals and society.
Microsoft Chairman and CEO Satya Nadella has said India could have the world's largest developer community by 2030, underscoring the country's growing pool of technology workers as a major advantage in the AI race.

Multiply Labs Raises $75 Million Series B to Close the Gap Between Drug Discovery and Drug Manufacturing
Series B funding will strengthen Multiply Labs' momentum scaling the robotic manufacturing platform turning AI-discovered drugs into treatments patients can receive.
SAN FRANCISCO, October 06, 2026--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Multiply Labs, the physical AI company automating some of the most complex manufacturing processes in medicine, today announced a $75 million Series B, bringing its total capital raised to over $100 million since its founding in 2016. The round was led by Dr. Patrick Soon-Shiong with NantWorks, with new investors AstraZeneca, Lingotto, Teradyne, and Strange Ventures, and returning investors Casdin Capital, Lux Capital, Fifty Years, Ora Global, and Founders Fund, among others.
Tens of billions of dollars are pouring into AI-drug discovery, but drug manufacturing timelines have remained largely the same. As AI accelerates drug discovery, manufacturing is becoming a critical constraint, determining how quickly—or slowly—new therapies reach the patients waiting for them. Some of the most complex processes in biomanufacturing remain largely manual, and a single contamination event can cost millions of dollars and delay access to life-saving medicine. Multiply Labs automates these processes with robotics, helping reduce contamination, increase manufacturing capacity, and close the gap between what AI can design and what patients can actually get.
Multiply Labs' robotic clusters integrate with a company's existing instruments and processes, without requiring a new facility or changes to already-validated practices. Each cluster automates the timed, repetitive steps of biologics manufacturing within an enclosed, GMP-compliant system, delivering a 74% reduction in cost per dose and up to 100 times more throughput than manual manufacturing. The system is autonomous, not just automated, meaning it learns, adapts, and runs continuously, removing the manual handoffs between process steps where contamination risk is highest.
"Robotics is the only way to deliver these therapies to patients at scale," said Fred Parietti, Co-Founder and CEO of Multiply Labs. "AI is designing more therapies than the industry will ever be able to manufacture. This funding lets us build the capacity to close that gap, so more of the patients who need these treatments can actually get them."
Beginning with cell and gene therapy and now expanding to advanced biologics, including antibodies, viral vectors, and mRNA, the company's platform is owned and operated directly by pharmaceutical and biologics companies rather than run as an outsourced service, giving manufacturers direct control over their production capacity. That trajectory is what drew this round's investor base.
